teaser: She wears court fashion, a faint smile, and gloves cut open to show her rings. Then you see the ledge.
review_notes:
Klimt's Judith I (1901, Belvedere, Vienna) is used as a later echo only; the lesson does not claim Klimt copied Cranach.
Political reading (Judith as an emblem for the Protestant princes; Schmalkaldic League formed 1531) is a common scholarly interpretation, not a documented commission.
'More than a dozen' surviving Judith versions from Cranach and workshop; versions in Vienna (Kunsthistorisches Museum), Kassel and Stuttgart.
Support and size: linden panel, about 89.5 x 62 cm; acquired by the Met in 1911 (Rogers Fund).
Cranach's businesses (pharmacy, wine license, printing) and several terms as mayor of Wittenberg.
Slit gloves showing rings as a period fashion.

lesson.text: Vienna, 1901. Gustav Klimt paints a woman with half-closed eyes, a wide gold collar tight around her throat, and a man's severed head pushed to the edge of the frame. He calls her Judith. Viewers were shocked that a Bible heroine could look so pleased with herself. Lucas Cranach had painted that same unsettling calm about 370 years earlier.

The story comes from the Book of Judith. An Assyrian army is starving her town into surrender. Judith, a young widow, puts on her finest clothes, walks into the enemy camp and charms its general, Holofernes. When he drinks himself to sleep in his tent, she takes his own sword and cuts off his head. By morning the army has fled.

Cranach skips all of that. No tent, no night, no servant with a sack. He shows only the aftermath: a woman, a head and a sword, on a ledge against black. It is built like a portrait, the kind a duchess might sit for, which makes the lower third a nasty surprise. Travel down the picture from the top.

lesson.title: From hair to ledge
lesson.text: A court portrait that turns into something else on the way down.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Pale skin, narrow eyes that slide off to one side, the corner of the mouth just lifted. Not triumph, not horror. She looks like someone who knows something you do not.

spots.title: Collar and chains
spots.text: A jeweled band clamps her throat, with heavy gold chains looped below it. A neck wrapped in gold, directly above a neck cut through: the rhyme is hard to miss.

spots.title: Fingers in his hair
spots.text: Her gloved fingers sink into his curls and hold the head in place, the way you might rest a hand on a cushion. There is no tension in the wrist at all.

spots.title: Holofernes
spots.text: Eyes not quite shut, mouth open, teeth showing. Under the beard the cut is painted as raw red flesh, and it sits at the front edge of the ledge, the part closest to you.

lesson.text: That calm is the whole point. For centuries Judith had stood for humility defeating pride, a small town beating an empire. Cranach keeps the virtue and adds a cool, courtly glamour. His heroine does not pray or tremble. She poses.

Cranach's workshop also sold pictures of Salome, the dancer who asked for the head of John the Baptist. The two women can look almost identical. The quick test: Judith holds a sword, Salome carries the head on a platter.

And consider what she wears. Nothing is ancient or biblical. The slashed sleeves with white lining pulled through the cuts, the stiff gold bodice, the net of pearls over her hair: this is high fashion at the court of Saxony around 1530, where Cranach was official painter. One detail of that fashion is easy to miss.
Her gloves have been cut open on purpose. Find the slits, and what shows through them.

spots.title: Rings through gloves
spots.text: Each finger of the pale glove is slit at the knuckle so the rings underneath can sparkle through. It was a real fashion: why hide your jewelry just because your hands are covered?

lesson.text: That ringed hand rests on the sword as lightly as the other rests on the hair. The blade lies flat, clean and gray, sliding out of the picture to the right. Later painters of this scene, Caravaggio and Artemisia Gentileschi among them, went for blood and struggle. Cranach wants elegance, and a chill.

Painting was only one of Cranach's trades. In the town of Wittenberg he owned a pharmacy, held a license to sell wine, ran a printing press and served several terms as mayor. He was one of the richest men in town.

Why so many Judiths around 1530? One likely reason is politics. The Protestant princes of Germany, Cranach's employers among them, felt threatened by the Catholic emperor and formed a defensive alliance in 1531. A small people standing up to a giant army was exactly the story they wanted on their walls.
The picture is painted on a panel of linden wood about 90 centimeters high (35 inches), a little under life size. The Metropolitan Museum bought it in 1911.

Demand was strong enough for the workshop to turn the subject out in series. More than a dozen versions survive, in Vienna, Kassel, Stuttgart and elsewhere, with the hat, the dress or the tilt of the head changed each time. What held them together was the master's design. Here it is, reduced to three lines.
A design simple enough to repeat, and strong enough to remember.

lines.label: The pyramid
lines.text: Her shoulders and puffed sleeves widen into a broad triangle with her face at the top. That stable shape is a large part of why she seems so untroubled.

lines.label: Two heads
lines.text: One head sits directly above the other, living over dead. Hers tips one way and his the other, like the two figures on a playing card.

lines.label: The blade
lines.text: A long gray stroke that underlines the whole portrait and slips off the right edge. It is the only straight line in a picture full of curls, chains and puffs.

lesson.text: A queen over a king, held in perfect balance. Now back to Vienna. Klimt's Judith hangs in the Belvedere, and one of Cranach's Judiths has long hung across town in the Kunsthistorisches Museum. Whether or not Klimt had her in mind, the idea was already old: a heroine is most disturbing when she is perfectly composed.

quiz.question: How does Judith kill Holofernes in the story?
options: She cuts off his head with his own sword
She sets fire to his tent
quiz.explanation: She beheads the sleeping general with his own sword.

quiz.question: What kind of clothes does Cranach give Judith?
quiz.explanation: She is dressed like a lady of the Saxon court where Cranach worked.

quiz.question: Why are her gloves slit at the knuckles?
options: They were torn in the struggle
To let her grip the sword
To show off the rings underneath
quiz.explanation: Cut gloves were a fashion that let rings show through.

quiz.question: How can you tell a Cranach Judith from a Cranach Salome?
options: Judith holds a sword, Salome a platter
quiz.explanation: The sword marks Judith, the platter marks Salome.

quiz.question: Which later Viennese painter made a famous Judith with a gold collar?

facts.text: Cranach shows the killing itself, inside the general's tent.
facts.explanation: He shows only the aftermath: a woman, a head and a sword against black.

facts.text: Besides painting, Cranach owned a pharmacy and served as mayor of Wittenberg.
facts.explanation: He ran several businesses and was one of the town's richest men.

facts.text: This is the only Judith that Cranach's workshop ever produced.
facts.explanation: More than a dozen versions survive in different museums.
